cohen_kappa.formula_reference_note: Point estimate: Cohen, J. (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 20(1), 37–46 (unweighted); Cohen, J. (1968). Weighted kappa: Nominal scale agreement with provision for scaled disagreement or partial credit. Psychological Bulletin, 70(4), 213–220 (linear/quadratic weighting; weight convention w_ij=1−|i−j|/(q−1) for linear, w_ij=1−(i−j)²/(q−1)² for quadratic, matching scikit-learn's own internal convention, verified by direct numerical comparison). Standard error, z, and p-value: Fleiss, J.L., Cohen, J., & Everitt, B.S. (1969). Large sample standard errors of kappa and weighted kappa. Psychological Bulletin, 72(5), 323–327, Equation 9 (the null-hypothesis, H0:κ=0 variance -- this module's exact implementation of Equation 9 was verified by reproducing the primary source's own worked numerical example, N=200, to six decimal places, and by external cross-validation against independent reference statistical software on a real N=86 dataset). Interpretation benchmarks: Landis, J.R., & Koch, G.G. (1977). The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data. Biometrics, 33(1), 159–174.
cohen_kappa.kappa_ci_note: Two standard errors from Fleiss, Cohen & Everitt (1969) are reported. The null-hypothesis SE (Equation 9, valid when kappa = 0) is used only for the z statistic and p-value. The confidence interval uses the general-purpose SE (Equation 8), which the authors give for setting confidence limits; z-basis and t-basis (df = n - 1) intervals are both shown.
cohen_kappa.interpretation_text: The Cohen's κ (κ = 0.413) indicates moderate inter-rater agreement among 2 raters rating 86 units (dichotomous (2 categories) data; Moderate (0.41–0.60)). Moderate agreement indicates reasonable but imperfect consistency. Acceptable for exploratory research; improvement is recommended for high-stakes assessment or publication purposes. Landis & Koch (1977) benchmarks: <0 Poor; 0.00–0.20 Slight; 0.21–0.40 Fair; 0.41–0.60 Moderate; 0.61–0.80 Substantial; 0.81–1.00 Almost Perfect.
cohen_kappa.formula_note: κ = (P_o − P_e) / (1 − P_e). P_o = observed proportion of agreement. P_e = Σ_c p_c(r1) × p_c(r2) = expected agreement by chance. SE for z and p: Fleiss, Cohen & Everitt (1969), Eq. 9 (H0: κ = 0); SE for the confidence interval: Eq. 8 of the same paper. Prevalence Index (PI) = |a − d| / n; Bias Index (BI) = (b − c) / n, from the 2×2 table a=both rate '1', b=rater1 '1'/rater2 '0', c=rater1 '0'/rater2 '1', d=both rate '0' (Byrt, Bishop, & Carlin, 1993). Reference: Cohen (1960). Educational and Psychological Measurement.

krippendorff.label: Unreliable (< 0.667 — Krippendorff recommends discarding data at this level)
krippendorff.interpretation_text: The Krippendorff's α (α = 0.414) indicates unreliable inter-rater agreement among 2 raters rating 86 units (nominal (unordered categorical) data; Unreliable (< 0.667 — Krippendorff recommends discarding data at this level)). Krippendorff (2004) recommends discarding data at this level rather than drawing conclusions from it -- the raters' classifications are not consistent enough to support substantive interpretation. Rater training and clearer operational definitions of the categories are strongly recommended before re-collecting these ratings. Krippendorff (2004) recommends α ≥ 0.800 for reliable data and considers α ≥ 0.667 the minimum acceptable threshold; he gives no finer breakdown below that threshold -- any value under 0.667 is treated as a reason to discard the data, not placed on a graded scale.
krippendorff.formula_note: α = 1 − D_o/D_e (Krippendorff, 2004). D_o = observed disagreement (mean pairwise distance within units). D_e = expected disagreement (mean pairwise distance across all values). Distance metric for nominal data: d(a,b) = 0 if a=b, else 1. 95% CI: percentile bootstrap over rated units (1,000 resamples of units with replacement, seed=42). Handles missing data and any number of raters. Thresholds: α≥0.800 reliable; 0.667≤α<0.800 tentatively acceptable; α<0.667 unreliable (Krippendorff, 2004).

percentage_agreement.interpretation_text: Percentage Agreement = 77.9% (95% CI [0.690, 0.869]) across 2 raters on 86 units. scott_pi.label: Moderate (0.41–0.60)
scott_pi.interpretation_text: Scott's π = 0.411 indicates moderate agreement between 2 raters on 86 units (dichotomous data; Moderate (0.41–0.60)). The result is moderate; acceptable for exploratory research. Scott's π uses averaged marginal proportions to estimate expected agreement, unlike Cohen's κ which uses the product of separate marginals — yielding slightly different estimates when rater marginals differ. Reference: Scott (1955).
scott_pi.dual_ci_note:
Two confidence intervals are reported for Scott's π, on two different, both-legitimate theoretical bases:
• z-basis (95% CI): [0.1891, 0.6326] — uses the standard normal critical value; the SE is the general-purpose large-sample variance of Fleiss’ kappa (Gwet, K.L. (2021). Educational and Psychological Measurement, 81(4), 781–790), which applies here because with two raters Fleiss’ kappa equals Scott’s π. The z-test and p-value use the null-hypothesis SE of Fleiss, Nee & Landis (1979) instead, which is valid only under H0: π = 0.
• t-basis (df=85): [0.1859, 0.6358] — a more conservative alternative (always at least as wide as the z-basis interval). Gwet (2021) evaluated this variance with Student's t on n − 1 degrees of freedom and reported coverage close to the nominal level.
The two intervals converge as n grows; report the basis that matches the convention of your field and cite its source.

brennan_prediger.label: Moderate (0.41–0.60)
brennan_prediger.interpretation_text: Brennan-Prediger coefficient = 0.558 indicates moderate agreement between 2 raters on 86 units (dichotomous, 2 categories; Moderate (0.41–0.60)). Chance agreement is fixed at P_e = 1/2 = 0.500, the value expected if raters used the 2 declared categories uniformly at random, so it does not depend on the observed category prevalence; the coefficient therefore depends on the declared number of categories q. With q = 2 it equals the prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa (Byrt, Bishop & Carlin, 1993). Reference: Brennan & Prediger (1981).
comparison_table: Product of each rater's own marginal proportions
Pooled (grand) marginal proportions across both raters
Uniform 1/q -- assumes all categories equally likely a priori
brennan_prediger.comparison_note: Brennan-Prediger, Cohen's κ, and Gwet's AC1 all take the same general form κ=(Po−Pe)/(1−Pe) and share the identical observed agreement Po; they differ only in how Pe (expected chance agreement) is modelled. Brennan-Prediger's uniform-probability Pe makes it immune to the prevalence and bias paradoxes that can distort Cohen's κ when category use is very unequal between or within raters -- but this comes at the cost of assuming a chance model (equal category probability) that may not reflect the actual rating task.
brennan_prediger.dual_ci_note:
Two confidence intervals are reported for Brennan-Prediger, on two different, both-legitimate theoretical bases:
• z-basis (95% CI): [0.3828, 0.7335] — uses the standard normal critical value; the SE is Cohen’s (1960) large-sample approximation (Educational and Psychological Measurement, 20(1), 37–46), which treats Pe as fixed; this holds exactly here because Pe = 1/q is set by the declared number of categories.
• t-basis (df=85): [0.3802, 0.7360] — a more conservative alternative (always at least as wide as the z-basis interval). Intervals with Student's t on n − 1 degrees of freedom are the convention of Gwet's (2014) inference framework as implemented in Stata's kappaetc command (Klein, D. (2018). The Stata Journal, 18(4), 871–901).
The two intervals converge as n grows; report the basis that matches the convention of your field and cite its source.

gwet_ac1.label: Substantial (0.61–0.80)
gwet_ac1.interpretation_text: Gwet's AC1 = 0.647 indicates substantial agreement among 2 raters rating 86 units (dichotomous (2 categories) data; Substantial (0.61–0.80)). Substantial agreement — generally acceptable for most research contexts. Variance estimated via jackknife. Note: Gwet's coefficients are more stable than Cohen's κ under extreme marginal distributions (prevalence paradox). Benchmarks: Landis & Koch (1977), applied here only as a conventional descriptive scale, not because it was derived for this coefficient -- Vach, W., & Gerke, O. (2023). Gwet's AC1 is not a substitute for Cohen's kappa: a comparison of basic properties. MethodsX, 10, 102212 argue AC1 and κ respond differently to prevalence (for a fixed observed agreement rate, AC1 rises as prevalence moves away from 0.5 while κ falls) and that AC1, unlike κ, can be nonzero even when raters show no association at all -- so a verbal scale calibrated for κ does not necessarily carry the same meaning for AC1/AC2.
gwet_ac1.formula_note: AC1 = (P_o − P_e) / (1 − P_e). P_e(AC1) = (1/(q−1)) × Σ_c π_c(1−π_c), where π_c = grand marginal proportion of category c, and q = user-declared number of categories in the coding scheme (not merely the count observed in this sample -- see Gwet, Handbook of Inter-Rater Reliability, 4th ed., Ch. 4). Gwet (2008) proposed this P_e to reduce the dependence of the coefficient on category prevalence. Variance: delete-one-unit jackknife (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). Reference: Gwet (2008). British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 61(1), 29–48.

weighted_kappa.interpretation_text: The Weighted Cohen's κ (quadratic) (κ = 0.351) indicates fair inter-rater agreement among 2 raters rating 86 units (ordinal (ordered categorical) data; Fair (0.21–0.40)). Agreement is fair but substantially influenced by chance. Rater calibration sessions and clearer operational definitions of rating categories are recommended before using these ratings for research. weighted_kappa.formula_note: κ_w = (Σ w_ij p_ij − Σ w_ij p_i· p_·j) / (1 − Σ w_ij p_i· p_·j) (Cohen, 1968), with agreement weights over the q categories of the declared scale: quadratic w_ij = 1 − (i−j)²/(q−1)², linear w_ij = 1 − |i−j|/(q−1). quadratic.label: Almost Perfect (0.81–1.00)
quadratic.interpretation_text: Gwet's AC2 = 0.938 indicates almost perfect agreement among 2 raters rating 86 units (ordinal (ordered categories) data; Almost Perfect (0.81–1.00)). quadratic.when_to_use: The most commonly used default weighting scheme; penalises disagreements in proportion to the SQUARE of their category distance, so distant disagreements are penalised disproportionately more than near ones. Appropriate as a general-purpose default for ordinal scales when there is no specific substantive reason to prefer a different decay pattern.

krippendorff.interpretation_text: The Krippendorff's α (α = 0.351) indicates unreliable inter-rater agreement among 4 raters rating 86 units (ordinal (ordered categorical) data; Unreliable (< 0.667 — Krippendorff recommends discarding data at this level)). Krippendorff (2004) recommends discarding data at this level rather than drawing conclusions from it -- the raters' classifications are not consistent enough to support substantive interpretation. Rater training and clearer operational definitions of the categories are strongly recommended before re-collecting these ratings. Krippendorff (2004) recommends α ≥ 0.800 for reliable data and considers α ≥ 0.667 the minimum acceptable threshold; he gives no finer breakdown below that threshold -- any value under 0.667 is treated as a reason to discard the data, not placed on a graded scale.
krippendorff.formula_note: α = 1 − D_o/D_e (Krippendorff, 2004). D_o = observed disagreement (mean pairwise distance within units). Handles missing data and any number of raters. Thresholds: α≥0.800 reliable; 0.667≤α<0.800 tentatively acceptable; α<0.667 unreliable (Krippendorff, 2004).

icc.interpretation_text: The ICC(2,1) (ICC = 0.429) indicates poor inter-rater agreement among 2 raters rating 86 units (interval/continuous data; Poor (<0.50)). Moderate agreement indicates reasonable but imperfect consistency. Acceptable for exploratory research; improvement is recommended for high-stakes assessment or publication purposes. Koo & Li (2016): Poor reliability (thresholds: >0.90 Excellent, 0.75–0.90 Good, 0.50–0.75 Moderate, <0.50 Poor).
icc.formula_note: Point estimates, F tests and p-values: pingouin intraclass_corr (Shrout & Fleiss, 1979; McGraw & Wong, 1996). ICC(2,1) [pingouin: ICC(A,1)]: two-way random effects, absolute agreement, single rater — PRIMARY index: use when each unit is rated by the same raters drawn randomly from a larger pool. ICC(2,k) [pingouin: ICC(A,k)]: absolute agreement for mean of k raters — use when you will average all raters' scores in practice. ICC(3,1) [pingouin: ICC(C,1)]: two-way mixed, consistency, single rater — use when the same fixed set of raters rates all units (no random sampling of raters). ICC(3,k) [pingouin: ICC(C,k)]: consistency for mean of k raters. Absolute agreement (ICC2) is stricter: it penalises systematic rater bias. Consistency (ICC3) does not. 95% CI via the F distribution (McGraw & Wong, 1996). Benchmarks — Koo & Li (2016): <0.50 Poor; 0.50–0.75 Moderate; 0.75–0.90 Good; >0.90 Excellent.

lin_ccc.label: Poor (<0.50)
lin_ccc.interpretation_text: Lin's Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC = 0.426) indicates poor concordance between 2 raters on 86 units (Poor (<0.50)). CCC simultaneously evaluates precision (Pearson r = 0.513) and accuracy (bias correction factor C_b = 0.830). A high Pearson r with low C_b indicates raters agree on rank order but differ systematically in absolute scoring (scale or location bias). CCC ≤ Pearson r always holds; the gap between them reflects systematic bias. Benchmarks (Koo & Li, 2016 adapted): CCC > 0.90 excellent; 0.75–0.90 good; 0.50–0.75 moderate; < 0.50 poor. Reference: Lin (1989, 1992) Biometrics; Lin, Hedayat, Sinha & Yang (2002) JASA; McBride (2005).
lin_ccc.formula_note: ρ_c = 2σ_xy / (σ_x² + σ_y² + (μ_x−μ_y)²) = ρ × C_b. ρ = Pearson correlation (precision); C_b = 2/(v + 1/v + u²) = bias correction factor (accuracy); v = σ_x/σ_y (scale shift); u = (μ_x−μ_y)/(σ_x·σ_y)^0.5 (location shift). 95% CI via Fisher z-transformation on ρ_c. Reference: Lin (1989). Biometrics, 45(1), 255–268.

Consistency (ICC3) does not. 95% CI via the F distribution (McGraw & Wong, 1996). Benchmarks — Koo & Li (2016): <0.50 Poor; 0.50–0.75 Moderate; 0.75–0.90 Good; >0.90 Excellent.

krippendorff.label: Unreliable (< 0.667 — Krippendorff recommends discarding data at this level)
krippendorff.interpretation_text: The Krippendorff's α (α = 0.525) indicates unreliable inter-rater agreement among 4 raters rating 86 units (interval/continuous data; Unreliable (< 0.667 — Krippendorff recommends discarding data at this level)). Krippendorff (2004) recommends discarding data at this level rather than drawing conclusions from it -- the raters' classifications are not consistent enough to support substantive interpretation. Rater training and clearer operational definitions of the categories are strongly recommended before re-collecting these ratings. Krippendorff (2004) recommends α ≥ 0.800 for reliable data and considers α ≥ 0.667 the minimum acceptable threshold; he gives no finer breakdown below that threshold -- any value under 0.667 is treated as a reason to discard the data, not placed on a graded scale.
krippendorff.formula_note: α = 1 − D_o/D_e (Krippendorff, 2004). D_o = observed disagreement (mean pairwise distance within units). D_e = expected disagreement (mean pairwise distance across all values). Distance metric for interval data: d(a,b) = (a−b)². 95% CI: percentile bootstrap over rated units (1,000 resamples of units with replacement, seed=42). Handles missing data and any number of raters. Thresholds: α≥0.800 reliable; 0.667≤α<0.800 tentatively acceptable; α<0.667 unreliable (Krippendorff, 2004).

percentage_agreement.interpretation_text: Percentage Agreement = 3.7% (95% CI [0.022, 0.052]) across 4 raters on 86 units. Percentage Agreement does not correct for chance, so it should always be reported alongside a chance-corrected coefficient (Cohen's κ, Gwet's AC1, or Krippendorff's α). It is reported here as a descriptive baseline. Reference: Stemler (2004). Practical Assessment, Research & Evaluation.
